teach.title: What it does
teach.say: Some questions do not ask for a fact; they ask what to do, and often expect no answer at all. Latin puts the verb in the subjunctive (the form Latin uses for wishes, purposes and what someone tells someone to do) and keeps the question mark. That is **the deliberative subjunctive (the 'what am I to do?' question: quid faciam?)**. It is almost always first person: *quid faciam?* what am I to do? *quō eāmus?* where are we to go?

check.ask: Is eāmus asking for a fact, or asking what to do?

teach.title: The 'I' form ends in -m
teach.say: The first person singular of the present subjunctive ends in **-m**. First-conjugation verbs (the *-āre* ones) take *-em* (*labōrō → labōrem*); the second, third and fourth take *-am* (*respondeō → respondeam*, *tollō → tollam*, *dormiō → dormiam*). That one ending carries the whole question.

check.ask: Put labōrō into the 'am I to …?' form.

teach.title: The 'we' form ends in -mus
teach.say: For 'are we to …?' the same subjunctive goes into the first person plural, ending in **-mus**: *emō → emāmus*, *dō → dēmus*, *dormiō → dormiāmus*. It is the ordinary 'let us' form of the verb, asked as a question instead of urged.

check.ask: Put emō into the 'are we to …?' form.

teach.title: Not the plain future
teach.say: In the third and fourth conjugations the future and the subjunctive can look alike, so the sense decides. *Quid faciēmus?* asks for a fact — what shall we do tomorrow? *Quid faciāmus?* asks for a decision — what are we to do? If the question is asking for advice, or throwing up its hands, it is deliberative.

check.ask: tollam could be 'I shall lift' or 'am I to lift'. Which is it here?

teach.title: For past time, the imperfect
teach.say: When the doubt was felt in the past, the same question moves into the imperfect subjunctive (the '-rem, -ret' subjunctive, built on the infinitive): *dīcere → dīcerem*, *facere → facerem*. *Quid ego miser tunc facerem?* — what was I, poor man, to do then?

check.ask: The doubt was felt in the past. Put dīcō into the imperfect subjunctive.

teach.title: Ask one yourself
teach.say: Now build the question. Choose the person — 'am I to' or 'are we to' — put the verb into the present subjunctive, and keep the question word in front: *quid … cōgitem?*, *utrum maneam an redeam?*

check.ask: Ask it: put cōgitō into the 'am I to …?' form.

core.text: A question that expects no answer because the speaker is at a loss uses **the deliberative subjunctive (the 'what am I to do?' question: quid faciam?)**. The verb is the present subjunctive (the 'may / let' form: veniat = let him come, may he come), usually first person: *Quid faciam?* what am I to do? *Quō eāmus?* where are we to go? In a past story the imperfect subjunctive: *quid facerem?* what was I to do? Latin name: *coniūnctīvus dēlīberātīvus*.
English: *What am I to do? What should I say? How could we live?* — a question about what ought to happen, not about what is happening.
Question word + first-person present subjunctive = 'am I to …?', 'should we …?'; the negative is nōn.

invented.en: What am I to say to my father?
Am I to stay or run away?

core.text: In the 3rd and 4th conjugation the first person singular is the same in the future (the 'will do' tense) and the present subjunctive: *faciam*, *vīvam*. Only the tone decides: a real 'what will I do?' against a helpless 'what am I to do?'. Other persons differ: *faciēs* is future, *faciās* subjunctive.

more.text: Also easy to confuse: put the same question after *nesciō* and it becomes an indirect question with the same subjunctive — *nesciō quid faciam*, I don't know what to do. Standing alone with a question mark, it is deliberative.

The learner's notes: a doubtful question, often expressing frustration, sometimes used for rhetorical effect — *Quis mē dīligat?* (who could ever love me?), *Quōmodo vīvam?* (how am I supposed to live?). Third-person deliberatives exist but are rare in the course.

The same form without a question is a wish or an exhortation (*vīvāmus, amēmus* — let us live, let us love); the question mark and a question word make it deliberative. Ørberg's chapter 29 has the merchant's *Quid faciam?* and the steersman's *Quōmodo vīvāmus sine pecūniā?*
